strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: editing real driving scenes through natural language while preserving scene structure and controlling vehicle behavior. The combination of explicit 3D representations, language-conditioned simulation, and video refinement forms a coherent and potentially useful system.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements over ChatSim and Cosmos, particularly in appearance alignment (82.19%) and behavior alignment (71.67%). The 26-participant user study also favors the proposed method, providing complementary evidence beyond automated metrics.

The ablations support several design choices. Behavior refinement increases joint success from 34.29% to 51.43% on challenging multi-object instructions, and video refinement reduces FVD from 589.41 to 467.20. Supplementary experiments additionally investigate grounding, counterfactual conditioning, and infeasible-instruction rejection.

The manuscript clearly attributes its major building blocks and provides agent prompts, behavior rules, test-scene identifiers, and runtime measurements. Qualitative examples illustrate the refinement benefits, and the acknowledged failures involving median barriers and changed vehicle appearance are informative.
weaknesses: The main evaluation leaves important measurement uncertainties unresolved. Behavior alignment requires recovering world-space trajectories from generated monocular videos, but the depth assumptions, camera-motion estimation, tracking failures, and treatment of edited ego trajectories are unspecified. Collision and off-road rates are judged by GPT-4o on sampled frames without validation against geometric or human annotations. Consequently, the very low violation rates in Table 1 do not yet provide convincing evidence of physical reliability.

The stronger multi-object experiment exposes a substantial remaining limitation: even after refinement, Table 2 reports 22.86% collisions, 14.29% off-road behavior, and only 51.43% overall success. These results use different instructions and direct trajectory evaluation, so they do not contradict Table 1, but they substantially qualify the broad traffic-realism claims. Moreover, Section 8.1.3 counts off-road behavior only when a majority of trajectory points fall outside road boundaries, potentially accepting significant shorter excursions.

The distinct contribution of the proposed agents is insufficiently isolated. Figure 16 prescribes fixed guidance-update rules, so the reviewer appears implementable as a deterministic controller. Comparing against no refinement does not establish an advantage over that controller or compute-matched resampling. Likewise, Table 5 does not separate counterfactual enumeration from simply augmenting the instruction with original behavior descriptions. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, these missing controls leave the claimed methodological novelty uncertain, although the integration itself has value.

The experimental scope is limited relative to the claims. Evaluation uses 30 selected scenes, with grounding tested on only 50 queries from five scenes. There are no uncertainty estimates, detailed results by operation or interaction complexity, or quantitative comparisons with the closely related multi-actor method ChatDyn. Table 8's categorical judgments about competing methods' quality cannot substitute for these comparisons. The small FID improvement over Cosmos, in particular, should not be described as significant without supporting uncertainty analysis.

The learned video-refinement component is not sufficiently reproducible: the training corpus, size, train/test separation, and several conditioning and optimization details are missing. Its ablation measures only FID/FVD despite the documented failure of changing requested vehicle type and color. Measuring instruction alignment, geometry, and structure preservation before and after refinement is necessary to establish the claimed balance between realism and controllability.

strengths: The framework addresses a useful computer-vision problem: language-controlled editing of real driving scenes while preserving scene structure. Integrating explicit scene graphs, multi-object trajectory simulation, and video refinement supports a meaningful range of editing operations.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements over ChatSim and Cosmos: appearance alignment reaches 82.19%, behavior alignment reaches 71.67%, and FVD improves to 467.20. The 26-participant user study and qualitative examples provide complementary support for the system’s practical value.

The ablations demonstrate benefits from individual components. Behavior refinement raises multi-object overall success from 34.29% to 51.43%, and video refinement improves both FID and FVD. Supplementary experiments also evaluate grounding and infeasible-instruction rejection.
The presentation is generally clear, acknowledges dependencies on existing methods, and supplies agent prompts, test-scene IDs, runtime measurements, and informative failure cases.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is insufficiently validated. Appearance alignment and traffic violations are judged using GPT-4o on sampled frames, without reporting agreement with independently annotated ground truth or sensitivity to sampling. Behavior alignment requires recovering world trajectories from generated videos, but the depth, camera-pose, and back-projection procedures are unspecified, particularly for edited ego motion. These omissions directly affect the credibility of the headline controllability and traffic-realism results.

Reliable multi-object simulation remains unestablished. On the harder 70-instruction test, the full method achieves only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collisions and 14.29% off-road cases. This does not contradict Table 1, which uses different instructions and evaluators, but it substantially qualifies the broad realism claims. Moreover, Section 8.1.3 flags off-road behavior only when a majority of trajectory points leave the road, potentially overlooking consequential shorter excursions.

The contribution beyond integrating existing components is not adequately isolated. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the system integration has merit, but the claimed novel reviewer follows explicit, fixed guidance-update rules in Figure 16. There is no comparison against implementing those rules directly or against equal-budget resampling with validation. Consequently, the reviewer ablation confounds the proposed feedback strategy with additional generation attempts.

The comparison set does not sufficiently test the multi-object contribution. ChatDyn is acknowledged as supporting language control and multi-object simulation in Table 8 but is not evaluated quantitatively. Binary judgments about competing methods’ photorealism and instruction alignment in that table cannot substitute for measurements on shared tasks.

The video-refinement ablation measures only visual quality, although refinement can undermine the explicit controls: Figure 11 shows a green convertible becoming a black sedan. Alignment, object identity, and trajectory preservation should also be evaluated before and after refinement to establish the claimed simultaneous improvement in realism and controllability.

Experimental reproducibility and generalization evidence are incomplete. The refinement training-set size, composition, and separation from test scenes are unspecified; the exact main-test instruction count and uncertainty estimates are absent. Thirty selected scenes and fifty grounding queries provide limited coverage, especially for open-vocabulary claims. Detailed prompts and scene IDs help, but do not resolve these gaps.

strengths: The main contribution is an integrated editing system, so Applied/Systems is more appropriate than Algorithms/General. On this basis, combining existing models is valuable: explicit scene graphs, language grounding, trajectory simulation, feedback, and video refinement provide a useful interface for several driving-scene editing operations.

Table 1 reports substantial improvements over ChatSim and Cosmos. Appearance alignment reaches 82.19% versus 46.25% for the strongest baseline, and behavior alignment reaches 71.67% versus 32.86%. Lower FVD and strong human preferences for instruction alignment and structure preservation provide complementary support.

The component experiments strengthen the empirical case. Behavior refinement improves overall trajectory success from 34.29% to 51.43%, video refinement reduces FVD from 589.41 to 467.20, and the supplementary grounding comparison reports a large accuracy advantage.

The pipeline is clearly explained, with useful qualitative examples, agent prompts, scene identifiers, runtime measurements, and explicit failure cases. Acknowledging median-barrier violations and appearance changes during refinement helps delineate the system's actual capabilities.
weaknesses: The central evaluation requires stronger validation. Table 1 measures collisions and off-road events using a VLM on sampled frames, without establishing agreement with geometric or human event annotations. Behavior evaluation reconstructs world trajectories from video tracks, but the required depth and camera-motion estimation are insufficiently specified, particularly for edited ego motion. These uncertainties directly affect the headline controllability and traffic-realism claims.

Reliable multi-object editing remains insufficiently demonstrated. On the harder 70-instruction benchmark, the complete method achieves only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates. This is a different task and evaluation protocol from Table 1, rather than a numerical contradiction, but it substantially qualifies the claim of consistently realistic trajectories. Furthermore, Section 8.1.3 counts off-road behavior only when a majority of trajectory points are outside road boundaries, overlooking shorter violations.

The ablations do not isolate the value of the proposed agentic reasoning from additional sampling and predetermined control rules. Figure 16 specifies essentially deterministic guidance updates. A compute-matched resampling baseline and a rule-based implementation of the same feedback policy would clarify what the reviewer agent contributes beyond repeated LangTraj execution. This matters even under a systems assessment because specialized agents are presented as a central innovation.

The video-refinement training data are insufficiently documented: dataset size, scene selection, and separation from the 30 evaluation scenes are not established. The paper provides training iterations and hardware, but these do not resolve reproducibility or possible train–test overlap. Refinement is ablated only for FID/FVD, despite the documented failure in which it changes the requested vehicle's type and color; alignment and structure should also be measured before and after refinement.

Experimental coverage is limited relative to the broad claims: 30 selected scenes from one dataset, primarily single-object instructions in the main comparison, and 50 grounding queries from five scenes with an IoU threshold of 0.2. Uncertainty estimates and detailed human-study allocation are absent, so small differences such as FID 32.85 versus 33.42 should not be described as established significant gains. The promising system merits consideration, but the unresolved evaluation and reproducibility concerns leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: editing real driving videos through object-specific language instructions while preserving scene structure and plausible interactions. The integration of explicit 3D scene graphs, language-conditioned trajectory generation, and diffusion-based harmonization is coherent and supports removal, replacement, insertion, and multi-object behavior editing.

The reported end-to-end improvements are substantial. In Table 1, appearance alignment reaches 82.19% versus 46.25% for Cosmos and 42.33% for ChatSim; behavior alignment reaches 71.67% versus 32.86% and 26.64%. FVD and structure preservation also improve, and the 26-participant preference study provides complementary human evidence.

The ablations support several design choices. Behavior refinement improves joint success from 34.29% to 51.43% on challenging multi-object instructions. Video review restores appearance alignment from 65.47% to 85.28% while retaining most of the diffusion model's visual-quality improvement. The supplementary coarse-rendering comparison demonstrates that the full improvement does not come solely from video diffusion.

The supplementary material provides useful agent prompts, behavior-generation rules, scene identifiers, and guidance equations. The paper also explicitly examines diffusion-induced geometric degradation and documents a median-barrier failure, making the limitations more informative than a generic disclaimer.
weaknesses: The central traffic-realism evidence needs stronger validation. Table 1 measures collisions and off-road events using GPT-4o on sampled frames, without establishing agreement with geometric checks or human annotations. The same model family also participates in editing and appearance evaluation, creating a risk of correlated judgments. Human preferences help, but do not establish incident-detection accuracy. Behavior alignment additionally depends on reconstructing world trajectories from edited images, yet the depth, camera-motion handling, and tracking-failure protocol are insufficiently specified, particularly for edited ego motion.

The stronger multi-object evaluation exposes substantial residual failures: Table 3 reports 22.86% collision, 14.29% off-road, and only 51.43% joint success after refinement. These results concern a different, harder setting than Table 1 and therefore are not contradictory, but they substantially qualify the claim of consistently realistic multi-object behavior. Moreover, Section 8.1 flags off-road behavior only when a majority of trajectory points lie outside road boundaries, potentially accepting consequential shorter excursions.

The distinctive contribution of agentic refinement is not sufficiently isolated. Figure 18 prescribes deterministic guidance-update rules, while Figure 19 similarly specifies parameter updates after visual judgments. Comparing one pass with up to five feedback iterations does not distinguish adaptive review from additional sampling or tuning. Compute-matched resampling, a deterministic behavior controller, and fixed or searched video-guidance settings would establish whether the proposed agents offer benefits beyond these simpler alternatives. This matters under the default Algorithms/General assessment, although the integrated system itself has clear value.

Experimental coverage and uncertainty remain limited. Evaluation uses 30 selected Waymo scenes with few pedestrians, and grounding uses only 50 queries with an IoU threshold of 0.2. Exact aggregate instruction counts, per-edit-category results, repeated-run variability, confidence intervals, and detailed human-study assignment procedures are absent. Comparisons cover ChatSim, Cosmos, and an image-editing/video-generation composition, but provide no quantitative comparison with the cited language-driven multi-actor method ChatDyn on their overlapping behavior-editing capability.

Important reproducibility details remain missing despite the extensive prompts. The video-refinement training corpus, its size, and its separation from the 30 evaluation scenes are not specified; the training schedule alone cannot establish generalization. The supplementary downstream detection result is encouraging but lacks a clear held-out evaluation protocol, training-budget controls, and comparisons with simpler augmentation. These omissions, together with the metric-validation and attribution concerns, leave the scientific case slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: language-controlled editing of real driving videos with object-level control and plausible interactions. The integration of explicit scene graphs, trajectory generation, and diffusion refinement is coherent and supports removal, insertion, replacement, and behavior editing.

The reported improvements are substantial. Table 1 shows appearance alignment of 82.19% versus 46.25% for Cosmos and 42.33% for ChatSim, alongside better behavior alignment and FVD. The 26-participant user study provides complementary evidence, particularly for instruction alignment and structure preservation.

The ablations provide meaningful evidence that refinement helps. Behavior refinement increases overall trajectory success from 34.29% to 51.43% (Table 3), while video review recovers appearance alignment from 65.47% to 85.28% with similar FID/FVD (Table 4). Supplementary comparisons also show that the coarse pipeline improves over ChatSim without video diffusion.

The supplement documents agent prompts, behavior rules, test scene IDs, and guidance equations. The hallucination analysis and median-barrier failure case appropriately acknowledge limitations rather than presenting only successful examples.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately validate the central traffic-realism claims. Table 1 estimates collisions and off-road incidents using GPT-4o on sampled frames, without reporting agreement with geometric ground truth or human incident annotations. Appearance alignment is also judged by the same model family used within the refinement pipeline, creating a risk of evaluator coupling. Tracking and back-projecting edited videos into world coordinates is insufficiently specified, especially for changed ego trajectories, occlusions, and tracking failures. The human preference study supports perceived quality but does not establish the accuracy of these measurements.

The claimed agentic contribution is not sufficiently isolated. Figure 18 specifies deterministic guidance updates from validation flags, while Figure 19 uses fixed parameter-update formulas following two visual judgments. The ablations compare refinement against no refinement, but omit equal-budget resampling, deterministic feedback controllers, and tuned fixed-guidance baselines. Consequently, the results establish the utility of additional refinement but not the necessity or distinctive benefit of the proposed reasoning agents. Likewise, Table 9 changes several components simultaneously and cannot attribute its gains specifically to the agentic architecture.

Traffic compliance remains substantially weaker than the broad conclusions suggest. On the harder multi-object setting, the full method achieves only 51.43% overall success, with 22.86% collision and 14.29% off-road rates (Table 3). Section 8.1 defines off-road failure only when a majority of trajectory points lie outside road boundaries, potentially overlooking serious shorter excursions. These results concern a different setting and protocol from Table 1, so they are not contradictory, but they limit claims of consistently realistic multi-object simulation.

Experimental coverage and uncertainty are insufficiently characterized. Evaluation uses 30 selected Waymo scenes with fewer pedestrians and human-filtered generated instructions, without per-operation results, repeated-run variability, or confidence intervals. Section 6.2 says Table 7 uses Table 1 instructions, yet its full-method values exactly reproduce the separate 70-instruction multi-object experiment in Table 3; the evaluation set needs clarification. The grounding experiment is also limited to 50 queries from five scenes and uses a permissive IoU > 0.2 threshold.

Important reproducibility details remain missing despite the extensive prompts. The diffusion fine-tuning data size, scene composition, and separation from evaluation scenes are not specified. Exact baseline checkpoints/configurations, evaluation prompts and sampling protocols, and several refinement initialization values are also unclear. These omissions impede both reproduction and assessment of comparison fairness.

The downstream experiment provides only preliminary evidence of practical impact. Table 11 reports small absolute detection improvements, but lacks a clearly described test split, variability, and controls for ordinary augmentation or additional real data. Overall, treating the submission as Algorithms/General, the promising integration and reported gains do not yet outweigh the evaluation-validity and contribution-attribution concerns.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: language-controlled editing of real driving videos while preserving scene structure and coordinating object behavior. The integration of explicit scene graphs, multimodal grounding, trajectory simulation, and diffusion refinement is coherent and supports a broad range of edits.

The reported improvements are substantial. Table 1 raises appearance alignment from Cosmos’s 46.25% to 82.19% and behavior alignment from 32.86% to 71.67%, while improving FVD and structural preservation. The 26-participant user study provides complementary evidence, particularly for instruction alignment and structure preservation.

The ablations support several design choices. Behavior refinement increases multi-object overall success from 34.29% to 51.43% (Table 3). Video review recovers appearance alignment from 65.47% to 85.28% while largely retaining diffusion’s visual-quality gains (Table 4). The coarse-output comparison with ChatSim also shows that improvements extend beyond diffusion harmonization.

The supplementary material provides substantial implementation detail, including agent prompts, behavioral constraints, guidance updates, and test-scene identifiers. The hallucination analysis and median-barrier failure example acknowledge meaningful limitations. Together, the demonstrated capabilities and component evidence support a borderline acceptance.
weaknesses: Evaluation independence and reliability need stronger validation. GPT-4o participates in the pipeline and evaluates appearance alignment and traffic violations, creating a risk of correlated judgment errors. Behavior evaluation also reuses the semantic rules employed by the reviewer. The human preference study helps, but does not establish the accuracy of these automated metrics. Pixel-to-world trajectory recovery, including depth and camera-motion handling, is insufficiently specified, especially for ego-trajectory edits.

The traffic-realism claims exceed the demonstrated reliability. On the harder multi-object evaluation, the full method still has 22.86% collision rate, 14.29% off-road rate, and only 51.43% overall success. These results use different instructions and measurements from Table 1 and therefore are not directly contradictory, but they materially qualify its near-zero violation rates. Moreover, Section 8.1 flags off-road behavior only when the majority of trajectory points leave road boundaries, potentially accepting substantial temporary departures.

The experiments do not fully isolate the value of agentic reasoning from additional computation and prescribed control rules. Figure 18 specifies deterministic guidance updates, while Figure 19 prescribes parameter increases from binary visual judgments. Comparisons against equal-budget resampling, fixed guidance schedules, and a simple controller using the same validation signals would clarify what the reviewers contribute beyond repeated generation. Likewise, outperforming ChatSim without diffusion does not isolate the architecture from differences in reconstruction and trajectory-generation tools.

The evaluation covers only 30 selected Waymo scenes, deliberately favoring fewer pedestrians, with eight-second front-camera clips and supplied maps and trajectories. Exact instruction counts, per-edit breakdowns, repeated-run variability, and confidence intervals are missing. The grounding experiment uses only 50 queries and a permissive IoU threshold of 0.2. These limitations constrain generalization claims and make small differences, such as the FID improvement over Cosmos, difficult to interpret.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed prompts: the diffusion fine-tuning dataset size and train/test separation are unclear, and exact model versions and several inference settings are unspecified. Section 6.2 describes Table 7 as using Table 1 instructions, although its full-method results exactly match the separate 70-instruction evaluation in Table 3; this needs clarification. The downstream detection experiment is encouraging but lacks sufficient split, training-budget, and augmentation-control details to establish a robust practical benefit.
